\chapter{Good Morning}
\label{ch:ta-good-morning}

\section[\ta{காலை} \ta{வணக்கம்}]{\ta{காலை} \ta{வணக்கம்} — \textquotedblleft{}morning greetings\textquotedblright{}}

\label{lesson:TA-C29-kaalai-vanakkam}



\begin{quote}
Every other language in this arc built its \textquotedblleft{}good morning\textquotedblright{} on a word meaning \textquotedblleft{}good\textquotedblright{} or \textquotedblleft{}auspicious.\textquotedblright{} Tamil does something completely different: it just puts its everyday greeting word after its word for \textquotedblleft{}morning.\textquotedblright{}
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \ta{காலை} \ta{வணக்கம்} — literally, \textquotedblleft{}morning greetings\textquotedblright{}}
\textbf{\ta{காலை} \ta{வணக்கம்}} (\textbf{kālai vaṇakkam}) — \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{good morning}\textquotedblright{} — is confirmed, by two independently-fetched sources, as Tamil's standard greeting for this time of day, used \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{from sunrise until around 11 AM}.\textquotedblright{} It's built from two words you already have: \textbf{\ta{காலை}} (already met, Chapter 26, \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{morning}\textquotedblright{}) plus \textbf{\ta{வணக்கம்}} (already met, Chapter 1, \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{reverence, homage}\textquotedblright{} — Tamil's everyday word for \textquotedblleft{}hello\textquotedblright{}). Literally: \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{morning salutations}.\textquotedblright{}

\begin{culture}
Here's the honest structural surprise: Hindi, Kannada, Telugu, and Malayalam each build their morning greeting on a \textbf{śubha}-equivalent word (\textquotedblleft{}good, auspicious\textquotedblright{}) plus a time-word. Tamil does something genuinely \textbf{different} — there's no \textquotedblleft{}good/auspicious\textquotedblright{} word here at all. It's simply \textbf{\ta{வணக்கம்}}, Tamil's own general greeting, specified with \textbf{\ta{காலை}} in front of it to mean \textquotedblleft{}morning\textquotedblright{} greetings specifically. Also be honest about a claim that didn't hold up: an initial search summary suggested a Sanskrit-borrowed word, \textquotedblleft{}suprabhatham,\textquotedblright{} serves as a casual alternative — but that claim appears on \textbf{neither} of the two pages actually fetched, so it's deliberately \textbf{not} asserted here.
\end{culture}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}kālai vaṇakkam\textquotedblright{} — \textquotedblleft{}good morning,\textquotedblright{} literally \textquotedblleft{}morning greetings\textquotedblright{}
  \item the honest structural surprise — no śubha-equivalent word here at all, unlike every other language in this arc
  \item the two pieces you already know — kālai (Chapter 26) + vaṇakkam (Chapter 1)
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item What two known words build \ta{காலை} \ta{வணக்கம்}? (\textbf{\ta{காலை}}, \textquotedblleft{}morning\textquotedblright{} + \textbf{\ta{வணக்கம்}}, \textquotedblleft{}reverence/hello.\textquotedblright{})
  \item Does it follow the śubha-equivalent + time-word pattern used by Hindi, Kannada, Telugu, and Malayalam? (\textbf{No} — \ta{காலை} simply specifies Tamil's own general greeting, \ta{வணக்கம்}.)
  \item Is \textquotedblleft{}suprabhatham\textquotedblright{} confirmed as a casual alternative? (\textbf{No} — neither fetched source supports that claim, so this lesson does not assert it.)
\end{itemize}
